papers.title: Quasiparticle Quality Factors in Superconducting Resonators: Effects of Bath Temperature and Readout Power
papers.abstract: The performance of superconducting resonators underpins a wide range of modern quantum technologies, yet their quality factor often deviates at low temperatures from standard Mattis-Bardeen predictions. This discrepancy is often attributed to nonthermal quasiparticles generated by microwave readout power, which limits the sensitivity of superconducting devices. We present a macroscopic model based on modified Rothwarf-Taylor equations that incorporates a power-dependent phonon generation term, providing an explicit relationship between quality factor, bath temperature and readout power. The model shows excellent agreement with temperature sweep measurements of NbN microstrip resonators with \b{eta}-Ta terminations over a wide dynamic range of readout power levels, accurately capturing the transition between thermally-dominated and microwave-induced loss regimes. This framework provides a predictive tool for optimizing superconducting resonators and advancing the design of high-Q devices for quantum sensing and quantum information processing.

summary.summary: This work extends the Rothwarf-Taylor equations with a microwave power-dependent quasiparticle generation term to model the quality factor of superconducting resonators as a function of bath temperature and readout power. Measurements on NbN microstrip resonators with β-Ta terminations over a 40 dB power dynamic range and temperatures up to $T_c/2$ show excellent agreement with the model across the low-temperature saturation plateau, crossover, and high-temperature exponential decay regimes.
summary.motivation: Superconducting resonators exhibit quality factors that deviate from Mattis-Bardeen predictions at low temperature, saturating rather than increasing; this is attributed to nonthermal quasiparticles generated by readout microwave power, which fundamentally limits device sensitivity.
summary.method: The authors modified the Rothwarf-Taylor equations to include an explicit power-dependent phonon generation term $\Gamma_r = \eta P_{qp}/(V\Delta)$, deriving a quartic equation for the normalized quasiparticle density $u = n_{qp}/n^*$ that can be solved numerically for any $(T_b, P_r)$ combination to predict the internal quality factor $Q_i$.
summary.result: Two NbN resonators (R1 and R2) with resonance frequencies of 3.7895 and 3.4290 GHz exhibited $Q_c \approx 19000$–21000 and $Q_r \approx 2500$–3400 at 100 mK, with quality factors spanning 40 dB in power and $T_b$ from 100 mK to $\sim 0.4$ K, all captured by the model using only a single temperature-independent loss parameter $Q_{other}$.

papers.title: A Superconducting Levitating Oscillator with < 1 $μ$Hz Resonance Linewidth
papers.abstract: Experiments aimed at quantifying the interface between quantum and classical physics necessarily require a high degree of isolation from the environment: wavefunction collapse and quantum gravity effects at laboratory scales are predicted to be very subtle. Ideally, such tests would be performed in a closed system at extremely low temperatures in order to rule out any external influence and thermal fluctuations. Cryogenic levitated macroscopic bodies are excellent candidates for an accurate laboratory approximation of such systems, as a tether to another body would violate the requirement for the system to be fully closed. Here we report a significant milestone on the way to a practically suitable approximation of such closed system. We have built a milligram-mass superconducting oscillator operating at millikelvin temperatures showing extremely low dissipation rate, with the oscillator ring-down time exceeding 110 hours. This corresponds to the resonance linewidth of less than 0.8 $μ$Hz. The experimental setup is highly tunable and is compatible with adiabatic nuclear demagnetisation, promising even lower temperatures and lower dissipation levels in the future. We demonstrate the capability of our device by measuring drag from $^3$He impurities in superfluid $^4$He at a level of $\sim10^{-8}$ with the drag force in the femtonewton range.

summary.summary: A superconducting lead sphere magnetically levitated in a millikelvin dilution refrigerator achieves a ring-down time exceeding 110 hours, corresponding to a resonance linewidth of $(0.76 ± 0.02)$ μHz and $T/τ ≈ 10^{-8}$ K s$^{-1}$. The system demonstrates femtonewton-scale force sensitivity by detecting drag from $^3$He impurities at the level of $ m{3 × 10^{-8}}$ in superfluid $^4$He, with prospects for reaching $T/τ ∼ 10^{-10}$ K s$^{-1}$ using adiabatic nuclear demagnetization.
summary.motivation: Testing quantum-gravity and wavefunction-collapse models at laboratory scales requires macroscopic mechanical oscillators with extreme isolation and coherence. Cryogenic levitated bodies offer closed-system approximations superior to tethered masses, motivating pursuit of record-low dissipation rates.
summary.method: A 6.33 mg lead-plated Delrin sphere (2 mm diameter, type-I superconductor) is levitated using opposing NbTi superconducting coils in a wet dilution refrigerator with vibration isolation at 5 mK. Position is detected via radio-frequency inductive coupling between transmitter and orthogonal receiver coils. Free oscillations are measured in vacuum and in liquid $^4$He over multiple days using Fourier spectral analysis.
summary.result: Vacuum measurements yield $τ = (114 ± 3)$ hours and $Δf = (0.76 ± 0.02)$ μHz; in superfluid $^4$He, drag from $^3$He impurities at $x_3 ≈ 4.2 × 10^{-8}$ produces $τ = 4 × 10^4$ s and drag force $F_D ∼ 3$ fN for 1 μm amplitude oscillations at 3 Hz.

papers.title: Quantum metrology via partial quantum error correction
papers.abstract: We introduce a method for error-corrected quantum metrology where only partial quantum error correction (QEC) is needed to suppress local noise and maintain the probe states' super-standard-quantum-limit (super-SQL) sensing performance. This stands in contrast to the existing QEC-assisted sensing schemes in Phys. Rev. Lett. 112, 080801 (2014) and Phys. Rev. Lett. 112, 150802 (2014), where a probe state is encoded into the logical subspace of a quantum code and error correction involves measurements on all checks of the code. Here, we encode the probe states into superpositions of energetically different states of the underlying quantum code. For our probe states, error correction using a subset of checks is enough to suppress noise both before and after phase imprinting. We analyze the tradeoff in noise suppression. For noise parallel to our phase imprinter of weight $l$, we achieve a suppression of $p^δ$ where $p$ is the noise strength and $δ= \lfloor (l+1)/2 \rfloor$. We propose an adaptive imprinter weight increasing strategy to maintain super-SQL performance as we scale up the system. In all our examples, checks and phase imprinters are chosen to be local operators avoiding non-local connectivity.

summary.summary: This work introduces partial quantum error correction (QEC) for metrology using CSS codes, where probe states are superpositions of different code sectors and only a subset of stabilizer checks are needed to suppress noise while maintaining super-SQL scaling. The method achieves polynomial suppression $p^\delta$ (with $\delta = \lfloor(l+1)/2\rfloor$) of parallel noise and an adaptive strategy to balance performance against both parallel and perpendicular noise.
summary.motivation: Full quantum error correction for metrology is resource-intensive; this work asks whether partial QEC suffices to preserve entanglement-enhanced sensing and protect against practical noise channels affecting probe state fidelity.
summary.method: Probe states are encoded as superpositions of energetically distinct eigenstates of CSS codes (specifically toric codes on square/honeycomb lattices and Bacon-Shor codes). Partial error correction uses only a subset of checks; phase imprinting is $U(\theta) = e^{i\theta\sum_j S_{Z,j}}$ with weight-$l$ stabilizers, and readout via a global symmetry operator. An adaptive strategy increases stabilizer weight $l(N)$ only when perpendicular-noise QFI drops to SQL.
summary.result: For toric codes on square lattices ($l=4$), $F_{q,Z} \propto (1-cp^2)^2 N_Z N_Z^2$ achieves super-SQL with $\delta=2$ noise suppression; for honeycomb lattices ($l=6$), $\delta=3$. The Bacon-Shor code maintains both $F_{q,X}$ and $F_{q,Z}$ above SQL up to noise strength $p < 0.09$ using adaptive weight growth, with advantage persisting to $N=10^7$ qubits despite $pN \gg 1$. Mixed $X/Z$ noise scaling: $F_{q,XZ} = F_{q,X}F_{q,Z}/(4N_Z^2)$ remains super-SQL when $\nu_X + \nu_Z > 3$.
